title: CPU & Fetch-Decode-Execute
tagline: The three-step loop a CPU repeats billions of times per second to run every program you use.

sections.content:
A CPU looks intimidating but its job is simple: over and over, fetch the next instruction from memory, figure out what it means, and carry it out. Everything — JavaScript engines, databases, video games — is built on that one loop running billions of times per second.

Understanding this cycle explains why cache misses hurt performance, why branch prediction matters, and what 'clock speed' actually measures.

  CU --> ALU["ALU\n(execute)"]
  ALU --> REG["Registers\n(fast storage)"]
  REG --> PC
sections.caption: Key CPU components and the data flow between them during one instruction cycle.

sections.title: A Cook Following a Recipe
sections.content: The Program Counter is your finger on the recipe page — it always points to the next step. Fetch means reading that step. Decode means understanding it ('chop the onion'). Execute means actually doing it. When done, your finger moves to the next line — the PC increments. Registers are ingredients already in your hands; RAM is the pantry. Grabbing from your hands is instant; running to the pantry takes time.

**CPU components**: The **Control Unit (CU)** orchestrates everything. The **ALU** (Arithmetic Logic Unit) does actual math and comparisons. **Registers** are a tiny set of ultra-fast named slots (e.g., rax, rbx on x86-64) — typically 16–32 of them, each holding one word (64 bits on modern CPUs). The **Program Counter (PC)** is a special register always holding the address of the next instruction. The **Instruction Register (IR)** holds the instruction currently being processed.

**The cycle**: (1) **Fetch** — read the instruction at the address in PC; load it into IR; increment PC. (2) **Decode** — the CU interprets the opcode field to know which operation to perform and which registers or memory locations are involved. (3) **Execute** — the ALU computes, or data moves between registers and memory, or the PC jumps to a new address for a branch.

**Clock and pipelining**: The clock is a crystal oscillator ticking at a fixed frequency (e.g., 3 GHz = 3 billion ticks/sec). Historically one instruction took several clock ticks. Modern CPUs **pipeline** — splitting the cycle into stages so that fetch, decode, and execute overlap for different instructions simultaneously, achieving close to one instruction per clock tick.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: pc++ is the fetch; the if/else chain is decode; the actual operation is execute. Notice how the PC increments automatically — just like a real CPU — unless a JUMP or HALT overrides it.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: Interview insight: 'Why is a cache miss expensive?' — Because the CPU must stall (or speculatively continue) while waiting ~100+ cycles for RAM. The fetch stage can't proceed without the instruction or data. Pipelining hides some latency, but a branch misprediction flushes the pipeline and wastes the already-fetched instructions — hence branch predictor importance.

items: Fetch-Decode-Execute is the fundamental CPU loop — it repeats for every instruction in every program.
The Program Counter (PC) always points to the next instruction; it auto-increments or jumps on branches.
Registers are the CPU's fastest storage (< 1 cycle); there are only a few dozen, each one word wide.
Clock speed measures ticks per second; pipelining lets multiple instructions overlap, achieving near 1 instruction/cycle.
Cache misses and branch mispredictions stall or flush the pipeline — the main source of modern CPU performance loss.

quiz.question: What does the Program Counter (PC) contain?
options: The result of the last arithmetic operation
The address of the next instruction to fetch
The number of clock cycles elapsed
quiz.explanation: The PC always holds the memory address of the next instruction to be fetched. It auto-increments after each fetch (or jumps on a branch).

quiz.question: What is the correct order of the fetch-decode-execute cycle?
quiz.explanation: Always: Fetch (read instruction from memory), Decode (interpret opcode), Execute (perform operation).

quiz.question: What is the role of the ALU?
quiz.explanation: The ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit) executes mathematical operations (add, subtract) and logical comparisons (AND, OR, compare).

quiz.question: What does 'pipelining' mean in CPU design?
options: Running one instruction at a time completely before starting the next
Overlapping fetch, decode, and execute stages for different instructions simultaneously
Storing frequently used instructions in cache
quiz.explanation: Pipelining splits the cycle into stages and overlaps them — while one instruction executes, the next is decoding and the one after is being fetched.

quiz.question: A CPU runs at 3 GHz. What does this mean?
options: It executes 3 billion instructions per second
Its clock oscillates 3 billion times per second
quiz.explanation: GHz measures clock frequency — ticks per second. Actual instructions per second depend on IPC (instructions per cycle), which is separate.

quiz.question: Which register holds the instruction currently being processed?
quiz.explanation: The IR (Instruction Register) latches the instruction fetched from memory so the Control Unit can decode it.

quiz.question: Why is a cache miss costly for CPU performance?
options: It causes the CPU to execute incorrect instructions
The CPU must wait many cycles for data from RAM, stalling the pipeline
quiz.explanation: RAM access takes ~100+ cycles vs. ~4 cycles for L1 cache. A stalled fetch means the pipeline cannot proceed, wasting cycles.

quiz.question: On a modern 64-bit CPU, how wide is each general-purpose register?
quiz.explanation: Modern 64-bit CPUs have 64-bit wide registers, holding values from 0 to 2⁶⁴−1. The '64-bit' in the CPU name refers to this register width.

quiz.question: What happens to the Program Counter during a branch instruction that is taken?
options: It is set to the branch target address
It is saved to the stack and then incremented
quiz.explanation: A taken branch overwrites the PC with the target address rather than incrementing it, redirecting execution flow.

quiz.question: What does the Control Unit (CU) do?
options: Interprets instruction opcodes and orchestrates the rest of the CPU
Connects the CPU to external RAM
quiz.explanation: The CU decodes the opcode field of the fetched instruction and generates control signals to direct the ALU, registers, and memory interfaces.
